title: By their fruits (Matthew 7:15–23)
hook: a good tree bears good fruit; watch what people do

segments.voice: Yesterday, the narrow gate: strait, meaning tight. Your line was the narrow way. Did you step out of the crowd once? Day two hundred fifty-nine, the end of another week.

Everyone has met this person. Great at talking. The perfect words at the meeting, the lovely post online, the warm speech at the dinner. And then you watch what actually happens. Who gets credit. Who gets left with the dishes. How they treat the waiter. After a while, you stop listening to the speech and start watching the hands. Jesus, nearly at the end of his sermon, warns about exactly this, and he gives a test so simple a child could use it. Look at the tree. Then look at what grows on it. Today, by their fruits.
screen: `THE PERFECT SPEECH.` → `WATCH THE HANDS.` → `LOOK AT THE TREE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a warning, in the King James Bible: "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves." That's where the phrase a wolf in sheep's clothing comes from. The disguise is good. You won't spot it from the outside. So how do you tell? "Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?" In Galilee, everyone knew thornbushes. They grow everywhere, and they can look green and full from a distance. But walk up close and look for grapes, and you won't find any. Then the rule: "Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit." The Greek word for fruit is karpos, and it's one of the sermon's favorite pictures: what a life actually produces over time. And then Jesus turns the test around, onto the people listening. "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven." He even describes people who say they did great religious things in his name, and he says he never knew them. That's sobering, and Christians have always taken it as aimed at insiders, not outsiders. The test isn't how religious someone sounds. It's what grows. Look back at this week: the birds and the lilies, the speck and the plank, ask, the golden rule, the narrow gate. Every one of them is about fruit, not talk. Not what you say you trust, but whether you sleep. Not what you say about judging, but where you look first.
screen: `SHEEP'S CLOTHING.` · `GRAPES OF THORNS?` · `NOT EVERY ONE THAT SAITH, LORD, LORD.` · `WHAT GROWS, NOT WHAT'S SAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the fruit of your week. Settle, and breathe. Don't ask what you meant to do. Ask what actually grew. One kind thing that happened because of you. One thing that went sour. Look at both honestly, the way you'd look at a tree in your yard, without shame and without spin. If you pray, you can offer both, the good fruit and the bad. The bell holds the time.
By their fruits. Not by the speech or the disguise, but by what grows over time.
Your line: know it by its fruit. Today, when someone's words and actions don't match, trust the actions. And check your own tree while you're at it. Day two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christians use this passage to test teachers and to examine their own lives, often at the end of a day or week, asking what their faith has actually produced.

fork.setup: someone gives a beautiful speech about goodness. you can't see inside them. what does Jesus say to watch?
options: the fruit: what their life produces.
fork.reveal: "Ye shall know them by their fruits." and he turns the same test on everyone listening.

original.note: Greek: fruit; what a life actually produces.

trapdoor: what you thought: a way to spot bad people.
what it means: judge a life by what grows from it, and apply the test to yourself first.
what a scholar hears: karpos, a favorite Gospel picture; 'Lord, Lord' as the insider's confession; and the sermon's week of fruit, not talk.
